title: New techno-authoritarian nightmare just dropped

Silicon Valley millionaires can't stop trying to build their own cities

Imagine a lush green walkable town 90 minutes north of San Francisco home to a small community of passionate, brilliant, and driven people who host regular group dinners, book clubs, pickup sports. There is no crime, transport around town is easy, and residents are never confronted with things like poverty or conflict.

This is the utopian dream that Devon Zuegel, a software engineer and a former director of product at GitHub is selling to people in her quest to build a new town north of San Francisco called Esmeralda.

“Our team has an exclusive option on a beautiful piece of land 90 mins north of SF, in California wine country,” she announced this past fall. “If you dream of living in a small town while being surrounded by creative, high-agency people, we’re building this for you… Imagine living on a college campus. You run into friends, and everyone is learning and creating side by side together. Why only live this way for 4 years? Wouldn't people of all ages thrive like that? Why don't more places like this exist?" 

Putting aside the very obvious reasons why many adults with families don't want to go back to college dorm life, Esmerelda, is just the latest offshoot of a movement by a group of extremist Silicon Valley tech billionaires to buy up land and establish a physical community in hopes of expanding what they call the "Network State."

The Network State is a group of privately governed communities that bypass traditional democratic controls. Though the idea is often marketed as a decentralized, community-driven alternative to a nation-state, a network state consolidates power among rich tech leaders and grants them authoritarian-like power over the communities they establish. 

Of course, the world is full of wealthy suburbs and tax havens for these billionaires to retreat to, but that's no longer enough. They want to build cities where they can escape democratic society altogether.

So far, these Silicon Valley figures, led primarily by crypto investor Balajis Srinivasan and far right venture capitalists Peter Thiel and Marc Andreessen, have made several attempts to construct their Network State both domestically and abroad.

Earlier this year, a group of influential tech entrepreneurs affiliated with the network state movement announced a plan called California Forever, which seeks to develop a new network state city in Solano County. There is Praxis, a “crypto commune” network state enthusiasts are seeking to establish in the Mediterranean, Telosa, a proposed "utopian" city of up to five million people that would be built somewhere in the U.S., Próspera, a Network State "charter city" in Honduras, and Liberland, a three-square-mile stretch of unclaimed land on the western bank of the Danube, about halfway between Zagreb and Belgrade. 

Share

Though these projects are sold to the public as community-driven utopian living, they ultimately aim to centralize control of an area, bypassing democratic processes to govern residents as they see fit. By gaining control over local regulations, policing, and land rights, these Silicon Valley billionaires are establishing footholds for a new era of corporate authoritarianism. 

Esmerelda’s founder is heavily affiliated with the Network State movement. Zuegel, who was formerly the editor in chief of the Stanford review, a right wing campus newspaper established by Peter Theil, is an avid follower of Srinivasan and his techno-fascist vision. She was one of the first speakers at Balaji's Network State conference in September and she visited Próspera in 2021.

Zuegel says that Esmerelda will be modeled after an “Italian hill town” and have “a culture of learning & building.” In the announcement video Zuegel says she wants to build the “Chautauqua of the west.” (As someone who grew up very close to Chautauqua it’s strange to hear a relatively generic suburb romanticized this way.)

Last summer, she hosted a pop up town in Healdsburg, CA that served as a sort of trial run for Esmerelda. The pop up was littered with longevity-obsessed tech people, AI entrepreneurs and (judging from the pictures) had very little diversity. If you want a town where community events include Grimes hosting a “Bio Acceleration rave,” Esmerelda may be the city for you.

Share

The funding behind Esmerelda is murky. Zuegel herself is not a billionaire and it's unclear where the money to purchase the land to establish Esmerelda is coming from. The website for Esmerelda says the endeavor is “backed by patient, values-aligned investors.” Zuegel also has seemingly no professional experience in real estate development.

Gil Duran, the reporter who has been leading coverage of the expansion of the Network State, pointed out that the land allocated for Esmerelda is technically part of an existing town in California called Cloverdale. Cloverdale is a scenic community in northern California with rolling vineyards, historic Victorian homes and small town charm. "It seems like there's some misunderstanding!" Zuegel posted in a reply on X a few months ago. "Esmeralda will be part of Cloverdale, not separate."

"I don't think the people of Cloverdale understand that the Network State is planting roots in their community, and along with that a lot of ideas about shifting governance, taking local power, and establishing some degree of autonomy over the area." Duran said. "I think that the more the residents of Cloverdale find out about these people, the more their concern will grow."

On Esmerelda’s website, however, Zuegel claims a groundswell of support from local residents. “Since we announced our plans to purchase the property this summer, we have received tremendous local support,” Zuegel writes. “The City Council, Chamber of Commerce, and City Manager were helpful and supportive of our ideas and interest in the site was a big part of our decision to move forward… One reason the City is excited about this project is that it will generate substantial property tax and TOT (Transient Occupancy Tax) for the town.”

In many of Zuegel's posts about Esmerelda, she emphasizes health and wellness. The community of people who participated in the pop up trial run of Esmerelda last summer overlap heavily with the Silicon Valley "don't die" longevity-obsessed tech movement. 

But while these people claim to be obsessed with longevity and health, plans for Esmerelda so far appear to include zero plans to mitigate the spread of disease. Nowhere are there any plans to build upgraded air filtration into buildings, or install new tools to limit the spread of airborne viruses like Covid that continue to wreak havoc on the American populace. Will masking, testing for sickness, and remaining home when ill be normalized in Esmerelda? Or will it just be more wellness raves and workshops by Theil fellows? 

"These people are all about eugenics shit," Duran said. The emergent culture of Esmeralda appears to be built on deeply individualistic ideas of health. In her posts, Zuegel emphasizes that the town is geared to "high-agency people,” a belief system that emphasizes personal responsibility and purports that individuals must take control of their circumstances and actively shape their environment. What this sort of ideology generally ignores, however, are the systemic challenges many people face. It doesn’t matter how “high agency” you are, if you’re poor and get COVID at a wellness rave and end up permanently disabled, you’re fucked.

Duran said that aside from the toxic ideology underpinning the Network State movement, "even if you strip away all the gobbling gook about governance and tech authoritarian fascism, you still have a scheme to use this massive amount of tech wealth to swallow up large amounts of land, and with land comes political power."

With near unlimited amounts of money, Silicon Valley leaders can continue their quest to buy up land and gain control over towns in order to further their mission.

"Whatever their vision is of the future," Duran said, "it seems to be pretty apocalyptic. They're building all these places to hide out with their own kind while everything else is left to fall apart."

One can only hope they don’t succeed, in which case, as one Twitter user put it, "the HBO doc about how this blows up is gonna be so good."
